items.title: Bacteria swap genes like trading cards
items.claim: Sexual reproduction is supposedly biology's great innovation for mixing genes. Bacteria don't bother. They share DNA fragments — including whole antibiotic-resistance genes — directly between unrelated species, sometimes across genera.

options.text: Useful mutations spread across the bacterial 'pan-genome' far faster than vertical inheritance allows — antibiotic resistance can jump from one species to another in a single transfer event
Bacteria only share genes within the same species
Horizontal transfer is too rare to matter

items.reveal_title: Three mechanisms keep the bacterial gene pool fluid
items.reveal:
Conjugation: two bacteria form a physical bridge (pilus) and transfer a plasmid.
Transformation: bacteria scoop up loose DNA from the environment.
Transduction: viruses (phages) accidentally package bacterial DNA and inject it into the next host.

The NDM-1 resistance gene, first found in Klebsiella in 2008, jumped via plasmids across at least 11 bacterial species and 4 continents within a decade. Genes encoding beta-lactamases (penicillin breakdown) appear in soil bacteria; clinical pathogens picked them up after antibiotics entered hospitals.

The 'tree of life' for bacteria isn't really a tree — it's a tangled net.
items.why: Evolution is taught as descent with modification along branching lineages. Bacterial evolution is reticular — sideways, not just downward.

items.title: Mosses spend most of their lives haploid — like permanent eggs
items.claim: Animals are diploid (two copies of each chromosome) and reduce to haploid (one copy) only briefly in sperm and eggs. Mosses live mostly as haploid (gametophyte) plants. The diploid sporophyte is a tiny stalk that grows from the haploid plant, makes spores, and dies.
items.prompt: What does alternation of generations mean?

options.text: Plants alternate between adult and juvenile forms

The life cycle alternates between a multicellular haploid stage (gametophyte) and a multicellular diploid stage (sporophyte); both are 'organisms' in their own right, unlike animals where only the diploid stage is recognisable as an individual
Genes alternate between being expressed and silent
Generations alternate between male and female

items.reveal:
The full plant life cycle: gametes (haploid, n) fuse to make a zygote (diploid, 2n) -> sporophyte (2n) develops -> meiosis -> spores (n) -> spores germinate into gametophytes (n) -> gametophytes make gametes (n) -> cycle repeats.

Mosses: gametophyte dominant (the leafy green plant). Sporophyte is the stalk with a capsule, attached to and dependent on the gametophyte.

Ferns: sporophyte dominant (the leafy plant). Gametophyte is a tiny independent heart-shaped prothallus, easy to miss.

Flowering plants: sporophyte hugely dominant (the tree, the grass). Gametophyte is microscopic — pollen grains (male, 3 cells) and embryo sacs inside ovules (female, 7-8 cells). Both are dependent on the sporophyte parent.

Evolutionary trend: gametophytes have become progressively smaller, more dependent, more protected. Flowering plants reduce them to barely-cellular structures.

In animals, only the diploid stage is multicellular; gametes are single cells. No alternation in the plant sense.
items.why: The 'plant' you see in your garden is one of two organisms in a single life cycle. The other organism — the gametophyte — has been reduced and hidden in flowering plants, but it's still there inside every pollen grain.

items.title: Information can flow from RNA back to DNA
items.claim: Crick's central dogma: DNA makes RNA makes protein. The arrow goes one way: DNA to RNA. But retroviruses — including HIV — carry an enzyme that copies their RNA genome back into DNA.
items.prompt: What does reverse transcription mean for the dogma?

options.text: The central dogma is wrong and discredited

Crick's original statement was about residue-level sequence transfer; reverse transcription does flow RNA-to-DNA, but the forbidden flow (protein-to-DNA) has never been observed — the dogma is more nuanced than the textbook version
Reverse transcription is a lab artefact

items.reveal_title: Crick's original dogma was more sophisticated than the cartoon
items.reveal:
Crick (1958) explicitly listed which residue-level transfers were possible (DNA to DNA, DNA to RNA, RNA to protein) and which were special transfers (RNA to RNA, RNA to DNA) — possible but not normally done. He also listed forbidden transfers (anything starting from protein).

Reverse transcriptase, discovered by Temin and Baltimore in 1970 (1975 Nobel), is the canonical 'special transfer'. HIV uses it to integrate into the host genome. Some retrotransposons in our own genomes do it constantly.

The forbidden transfers (protein to DNA, protein to RNA, protein to protein) remain forbidden. The dogma, taken literally as Crick wrote it, still stands.
items.why: Pop science presents 'the central dogma' as a rigid one-way arrow. The real dogma is a constraint on which directions sequence information can flow in, and reverse transcription was always allowed.
